title: Extracranial meningiomas concurrently found in the lung and vertebral bone: a case report
case_prompt:
A 40-year-old woman in her usual state of health was incidentally found, on routine medical examination, to have a 1.2-cm nodule in the right lower lobe of the lung. She had no symptoms, her family history was noncontributory, and physical and laboratory examinations were unremarkable. A CT scan of the chest confirmed a well-circumscribed pulmonary nodule. Concurrent lumbar MRI showed a lytic lesion in the left transverse process of the fifth lumbar vertebra, confined to bone and separate from the spinal canal. Initial biopsy specimens of both lesions showed a bland spindle cell neoplasm, but were too small for definitive diagnosis. 

Over the next 5 years, both lesions increased slightly in size. The patient underwent video-assisted thoracic surgery for the pulmonary lesion and curettage of the vertebral lesion. The lung specimen was a 13-mm well-circumscribed solid lesion composed of fascicles of bland spindle or polygonal cells without necrosis or mitoses. The tumor cells contained intranuclear cytoplasmic inclusions. Immunohistochemical studies showed that the cells were positive for epithelial membrane antigen, D2-40, progesterone receptor, vimentin, and S100 antigen, and negative for alpha-smooth muscle actin; the Ki-67 labeling index was approximately 1.5%. The vertebral lesion demonstrated identical morphology and immunoprofile.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Consideration of multiple metastases from an unknown primary — “The patient was placed under close observation with suspicion of multiple metastases from an unknown primary tumor.”  
2. Primary pulmonary leiomyoma — “Primary leiomyoma, which arises in the bronchial wall, is also composed of bland and eosinophilic spindle cells. The location of the lesion will help in discrimination.”  
3. Metastasizing uterine leiomyoma — “A history of hysterectomy for uterine leiomyoma is essential for the diagnosis.”  
4. Intrapulmonary thymoma — “The intralesional fibrous septa and/or intralesional lymphocytic infiltrate, which typify thymoma, will facilitate correct diagnosis.”  
5. Solitary fibrous tumor — “Branched intralesional blood vessels resembling moose antlers and/or a so-called patternless pattern of the tumor cells are absent in meningiomas.”  
6. Metastatic meningioma from an intracranial source — “The patient showed no evidence of a tumor on imaging examinations of the head and neck.”  
7. Primary ectopic meningioma — “Immunohistochemical examinations will clearly discriminate the aforementioned lesions when pathologists consider the possibility of meningioma (Table 2).”
